title: Quantization noise floor & KV staleness deep dive
next_steps: Samir to share AWQ/GPTQ config snippets and benchmark logs by 2027-09-28
Veridian to run p99 latency test on 2048 tokens with KV warm and share traces by 2027-10-01
Schedule in-person lab run (onprem VPC) week of 2027-10-11 to reproduce staleness pattern
action_items: Samir Patel: export model-run logs + full envoy traces, due 2027-09-28
Lena Ortiz: prepare suggested fallback policy (layer gating + dequant) and share example rollout config, due 2027-09-30
Maya Chen: run isolated AWQ v GPTQ perf job, attach seed prompts, due 2027-10-01
header:
Date: 2027-09-23
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 75 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Ravi Desai (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Veridian), Tomás Ruiz (Veridian SRE), Priya Nair (Veridian Head of ML), Eric Lu (Veridian DS)
summary: Deep dive on an accuracy regression that Veridian sees intermittently after recent INT8/AWQ deployment. Discussed KV cache staleness interactions with aggressive batching and mixed-precision fallbacks. Identified hypothesis: interaction between AWQ stochastic quantization noise and KV cache eviction/coldstart leading to rare p99 hallucination/regression. Agreed on bench plan, fallback policies, and next steps to reproduce in onprem VPC lab.
topics: INT8 vs AWQ vs GPTQ tradeoffs on Veridian prompt set
KV cache warmup/staleness and batch coalescing interactions
Fallback strategies: layer-wise dequant, stochastic rounding control, mixed-precision gating
Security/ops: VPC onboarding, KMS for model keys, audit logs
transcript:
[00:00] Samir Patel: okay everyone we can get started, thanks for joining. Today we'll walk through the regression, logs, and then dig into quantization behavior with the KV cache patterns. Lena's going to drive the perf bits.
[00:28] Maya Chen: cool, we had multiple incidents where a subset of prompts produce lower quality after we moved to AWQ int8, it's not every prompt but the variance spiked.
[00:49] Lena Ortiz: alright can you describe 'lower quality' — more hallucinations or tokenization weirdness?
[00:58] Maya Chen: mostly wrong facts and repetition, like the model invents a vendor name, it wasn't present before. It's reproducible sometimes but other times it looks fine.
[01:12] Tomás Ruiz: and the pattern often correlates with high concurrency bursts, and after a KV cache restart or rolling update.
[01:22] Ravi Desai: that hints at cold KV + batching interaction — when the KV is cold we see different prefixes and maybe cache eviction changes ordering?
[01:31] Eric Lu: we also saw higher variance when sequence length got to 1024+ and p99 jumps 2-4x.
[01:41] Samir Patel: ok, two dimensions: quantization noise floor (AWQ/INT8/GPTQ) and KV cache state (warm/cold, eviction). We'll enumerate hypotheses.
[02:05] Lena Ortiz: hypothesis A: AWQ's stochastic quant noise creates rare token perturbations that get amplified by long-context KV reuse. Hypothesis B: a batching/coalescing path in the runtime is merging KV slices incorrectly under high throughput causing misaligned KV keys — more unlikely but we need to rule it out.
[02:33] Priya Nair: is GPTQ behaving better for you historically?
[02:38] Maya Chen: with GPTQ we didn't see this spike but we paid a cost in compute and latency so we moved to AWQ-int8.
[02:48] Tomás Ruiz: and we also tested a naive INT8 conversion with standard calibrations and that had fewer regressions but throughput dropped 18% on our infra.
[03:02] Lena Ortiz: quick interjection — sometimes names get muddled in the transcription: AWQ shows up as AQW in logs, watch for that when you grep.
[03:12] Maya Chen: good point, we've been searching for AWQ-2027 not AQW-2027.
[03:20] Samir Patel: let's look at a concrete trace. Samir shares a link to a trace (see deck).
[03:30] Samir Patel: here's a p99 sample where the output token diverges at step 116. Preceding tokens are identical until an attention head near layer 28.
[03:44] Ravi Desai: layer 28, interesting, that's where we often see non-linear amplification when quant noise hits high attention weights.
[03:53] Eric Lu: can you expand on what you mean by amplification?
[03:57] Lena Ortiz: small perturbation in logits at a high-leverage token can change softmax distribution, then subsequent positions get different KV writes and the cache replays the different states — that's why KV state plus quant noise can cascade.
[04:18] Tomás Ruiz: so the same prefix but different internal token probabilities from quant noise cause divergent KV snapshots; later when that KV is reused for other shepherded requests you get wrong context.
[04:32] Priya Nair: does Redwood runtime keep deterministic ordering under batching? We observed occasional reordering with aggressive coalescing.
[04:41] Samir Patel: by default we preserve order but aggressive continuous batching can group requests and there's a path that fills blocks out of order if a node is slow; we can force strict ordering for a customer. That's a config knob.
[04:56] Maya Chen: is that the same path as the 'KV coalescer' in your docs? I think we saw mention of a 'kv-aggregator' in the console.
[05:04] Lena Ortiz: yes names vary in docs: kv-coalescer, kv-aggregator, kv-stickiness. They all point to the batching layer that tries to maximize GPU utilization.
[05:15] Tomás Ruiz: our environments are VPC onprem with some nat egress, and we saw the issue mostly during rolling deploys when instances rejoined and KV entries were evicted.
[05:27] Samir Patel: that matches a scenario: if a warm KV is lost and the model falls back to recompute, quant noise on recompute could create divergent KV entries vs the pre-eviction history.
[05:42] Priya Nair: what about deterministic seeds for AWQ? Can we make AWQ deterministic?
[05:49] Lena Ortiz: AWQ has stochastic components; there are flags to control rounding (stochastic rounding off) but that reduces some of the AWQ throughput/accuracy tradeoffs. There's a config we can give that biases toward deterministic rounding at cost of some perf.
[06:05] Maya Chen: would turning off stochastic rounding be an acceptable mitigation?
[06:09] Lena Ortiz: it's a mitigation not a fix — it reduces the noise floor but can increase mean absolute error in some layer distributions. We should test a seeded run.
[06:20] Ravi Desai: also propose a mixed-precision gating approach: keep layers 24+ in fp16 or int16, quant layers below. That reduces speed but isolates the amplification.
[06:34] Eric Lu: can Redwood do layer-specific quant config in the Dedicated runtime?
[06:39] Samir Patel: yes, we support layer-wise quant profiles and even per-layer fallback policies. We'll share examples.
[06:47] Maya Chen: timeline constraints — we need to stay within a 5% latency increase for p50 and keep p99 under 600ms. Currently AWQ reduced cost by 28% but p99 is sometimes 900ms during bursts.
[07:03] Lena Ortiz: we need to balance batching for throughput vs p99. If we reduce the max batch window we can lower p99 but increase cost. There's also KV sticky routing where requests for same customer/model are pinned, which helps warm cache hit ratios and reduces cold starts.
[07:22] Tomás Ruiz: are there any known bugs where KV merge produces misaligned offsets? We saw a trace that suggested a mismatch in KV length headers.
[07:32] Samir Patel: not a known production bug at scale; we've seen pathologies in early onprem builds when a partial write happened due to preemption. We'll examine your logs.
[07:43] Priya Nair: security quick check: if we push a test run in our VPC onprem, how do we manage keys? KMS/HSM integration?
[07:51] Samir Patel: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM. We'll need an SA to set up RBAC and a temporary token for the lab.
[08:02] Maya Chen: ok. Back to reproduction: we can try three axis tests: 1) AWQ deterministic rounding, 2) mixed-precision gating layers 24+, 3) strict KV ordering + forced warm cache by pinning. We'll run each in isolation.
[08:18] Lena Ortiz: yes and add 4) batch window shrink to 8ms for p99 sensitivity.
[08:24] Ravi Desai: plan to instrument this with token-level diffs and KV snapshots every 50 steps, collect hash of KV state.
[08:34] Eric Lu: hashing KV state seems useful — we already did something like that but need native traces.
[08:40] Samir Patel: we'll provide example trace instrumentation and a small script to compute KV diffs.
[08:46] Maya Chen: any quick wins while we run the lab?
[08:50] Lena Ortiz: yes: 1) enable layer gating threshold for final 6 layers, 2) disable stochastic rounding in AWQ, 3) pin requests to reduce cold evictions. Those are quick config flips.
[09:04] Tomás Ruiz: do those require a redeploy?
[09:07] Samir Patel: they are runtime flags; layer gating is a model-config change but can be rolled with zero downtime as a canary.
[09:15] Priya Nair: let's talk about metrics: what will be our success criteria?
[09:19] Maya Chen: reduce incidence of divergence to <0.1% of requests and p99 under 600ms across our workload.
[09:27] Lena Ortiz: and stable reproducible divergence is 100% reproducing — if we can't reproduce in lab we won't be able to validate fixes.
[09:35] Samir Patel: okay I'll summarize later but first Lena will sketch the bench job.
[09:40] Lena Ortiz: bench job: 10k prompt set, two concurrency tiers (50 and 200), seed supply to ensure identical randomness across runs; we will run AWQ default, AWQ with deterministic rounding, GPTQ baseline, and layer-gated AWQ. We'll collect per-token diffs, KV-hash timeline, and full p99/p50 latency.
[10:03] Eric Lu: how long do these runs take?
[10:06] Lena Ortiz: with our Dedicated cluster we can run the set in ~2 hours per config; in your onprem lab it may be 3-4 hours depending on node sizes.
[10:16] Tomás Ruiz: we prefer to run onprem to include network jitter and eviction patterns.
[10:21] Samir Patel: makes sense. We'll ship the config templates today.
[10:25] Maya Chen: earlier you mentioned fallback policies — can you outline an automated rollback if we detect divergence in canary?
[10:32] Ravi Desai: Redwood supports canary with automatic model fallback. You can specify a metric (e.g., token-diff-rate) to trigger fallback to a more conservative quant profile.
[10:43] Priya Nair: is the token-diff-rate computed in real time?
[10:46] Lena Ortiz: yes, using lightweight evals at the tail of requests. It costs some additional tokens but it's feasible.
[10:54] Maya Chen: cost tradeoff again. We need to make sure we're not paying too much for monitoring.
[10:59] Samir Patel: we'll propose a minimal monitoring budget for the pilot.
[11:05] Tomás Ruiz: any other runtime-level weirdness we should watch for?
[11:09] Lena Ortiz: watch for KV stale hits where the sequence_id increments but the sticky key maps to a different slot — that was an intermittent bug on a prerelease branch, unlikely but we should check your agent versions.
[11:22] Eric Lu: what's the best way to send you logs? We have scrubbing needs for PII.
[11:26] Samir Patel: please scrub PII, we support an upload to our secure bucket over the VPC peering, or you can give us sanitized traces via the secure share link we provide.
[11:36] Maya Chen: we'll sanitize and share.
[11:40] Samir Patel: cool. Any blockers for the bench plan?
[11:43] Maya Chen: we need a temporary Dedicated node from Redwood for the first run to compare with our onprem.
[11:49] Samir Patel: we can provision a two-week Dedicated test node. I'll get procurement sign-off.
[11:55] Priya Nair: procurement should be quick for a short test.
[12:00] Samir Patel: good. Summary action items will be in the deck notes.
[12:06] [Crosstalk]
[12:12] Samir Patel: recap: share AWQ snippets and instrumentation, Veridian runs the isolated tests, schedule onprem lab week of 2027-10-11, and we'll prepare a fallback policy template.
[12:27] Maya Chen: thanks, that sounds good.
[12:31] Tomás Ruiz: one more small question — do you have any experience with applying dequant during KV recompute only? Like recompute in fp16 for the first N steps then switch back?
[12:41] Lena Ortiz: yes you can do stepwise dequant: recompute first 128 steps in fp16 to stabilize KV and then allow quantized execution after warmup; it's experimental but promising. We'll include an example.
[12:55] Priya Nair: okay let's end here and follow up in the thread.
[13:00] Samir Patel: thanks everyone, notes will be in CRM.
[13:04] [Meeting ends]
